title: Finite character Fourier kernel over a splitting field
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $N\ge1$ be an integer with $N\cdot1_k\ne0$, and let $H$ be a finite abelian group of order $N$. Let $C$ be a finite cyclic group of order $N$ (a group generated by one element), and let $\iota:C\hookrightarrow k^\times$ be an injective group homomorphism. Put $X=\operatorname{Hom}(H,C)$, the finite group of group homomorphisms with pointwise multiplication. For every $h\in H$ one has $$\sum_{\chi\in X}\iota(\chi(h))^{-1}=\begin{cases}N\cdot1_k,&h=1,\\0,&h\ne1.\end{cases}$$

source.place: VIII Lemma 5.3.5, proof, printed p.124 (PDF p.130): the diagonalization and character-averaging paragraphs. The finite character-sum identity is the scalar Fourier input to the diagonalization, expanded by the worker; it is not explicitly stated in the source.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-finite-additive-group-card-annihilator] to the additive notation for $H$ and $C$ (the operation is unchanged, its name is addition). Translating back gives $g^N=1$ for every $g\in H$ or $C$. Let $e$ be the least positive integer annihilating $H$; it exists since $N$ does. Divide $N=qe+r$ with $0\le r<e$. For every $g\in H$, $g^r=g^N(g^e)^{-q}=1$. If $r>0$, this contradicts minimality of $e$; hence $r=0$ and $e\mid N$.

source.place: VIII Lemma 5.3.5, proof, printed p.124 (PDF p.130): scalar character-duality and averaging input, expanded explicitly by Q28; Mathlib finite abelian duality supplies the non-elementary inputs.

proof.text: Choose a generator $c$ of $C$. Its order is $N$: if its least positive period is $r$, the distinct powers $1,c,\ldots,c^{r-1}$ exhaust $C$, so $r=|C|=N$. Thus $z=\iota(c)$ also has order $N$. All $N$ elements of $\iota(C)$ belong to $\mu_N(k)$. By [lem-exc-field-roots-cyclic-bound], this latter group has at most $N$ elements, so $\iota(C)=\mu_N(k)$. Write $N=ed$ with $d>0$. Then $z^d$ has order $e$, since $(z^d)^b=1$ if and only if $N\mid db$, equivalently $e\mid b$. The same cited node with $r=e$ gives cyclicity of $\mu_e(k)$. Hence the splitting hypotheses for exponent $e$ hold over $k$.

proof.text: Put $H^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}(H,k^\times)$. Composition with $\iota$ gives a bijection $X\longrightarrow H^\vee$. It is injective since $\iota$ is injective; it is surjective because, for $\alpha:H\to k^\times$, $\alpha(g)^N=\alpha(g^N)=1$ for every $g$, so all values lie in $\mu_N(k)=\iota(C)$. Taking the unique preimage in $C$ preserves multiplication by injectivity of $\iota$, and defines the inverse homomorphism. Apply [lem-per-finite-character-dual-cardinality] with $E=H$ and the exponent-$e$ splitting verified in Step 2. It gives $|H^\vee|=|H|=N$, hence $|X|=N$.

proof.text: For $h=1$, every summand is $1$, and Step 3 gives the sum $N\cdot1_k$. For $h\ne1$, let $S=\sum_{\chi\in X}\iota(\chi(h))^{-1}$ and choose $\chi_0$ as in Step 4. Multiplication $\chi\mapsto\chi_0\chi$ permutes $X$, with inverse multiplication by $\chi_0^{-1}$. Reindexing the finite sum and distributing multiplication gives $S=\sum_{\chi\in X}\iota((\chi_0\chi)(h))^{-1}=\iota(\chi_0(h))^{-1}S$. Thus $(1-\iota(\chi_0(h))^{-1})S=0$. Its first factor is nonzero by Step 4, and a field has no zero divisors, so $S=0$. These are exactly the two stated cases.
